title: (fix) O3-6135: Don't report extension config keys as unknown before the module has loaded
body:

## Summary

**Problem** 

Apps that render extensions log `Unknown config key '<module>.<key>' provided. Ignoring.` in the console for keys the module does declare in its schema. The value is still read correctly, so the warning is false, but it shows up on most pages for any module whose extension mounts before the module itself has loaded.

**Root cause.** 

`renderExtension` registers the extension with the extension store (`esm-extensions/src/render.ts`) before it awaits the bundle. That synchronously triggers `computeExtensionConfig`, which runs `validateStructure` against the module's schema. At that point the module only has the implicit schema `registerApp` gives every app, so every top-level key it declares looks unknown. `computeModuleConfig` already holds back structural validation until the module has loaded; `computeExtensionConfig` didn't.

Extensions that define their own config schema hit this too. `defineConfigSchema` marks a module loaded, and modules such as primary-navigation and patient-flags call it from `startupApp` before reaching `defineExtensionConfigSchema`. In that window, the extension's slot `configure` keys were checked against the module schema.

**Fix** 

In `computeExtensionConfig`, skip `validateStructure` for an extension without its own schema until its module has finished starting. A new `moduleStarted` flag tracks this. Only `registerModuleLoad` sets it, once `startupApp` has resolved, so unlike `moduleLoaded` it stays false while `startupApp` is still defining extension schemas. Whether the module has started is added to the extension config cache key, so a module that never defines a schema is still validated once it starts. Module config still waits on `moduleLoaded`, as before.

**Tests** 

Five new tests in `module-config.test.ts`:
- no unknown-key error before the module defines its schema, and the provided value is used afterwards
- a key missing from the schema is still reported once the module defines its schema
- a key is still reported once a module without a schema has loaded
- a wrong-type value (and a failing validator) is still reported once the schema is defined
- an extension's slot `configure` keys aren't checked against the module schema while its module starts up, and a key the extension's own schema doesn't declare is still reported as soon as `defineExtensionConfigSchema` runs

## Summary

This PR replaces `jwalton/gh-docker-logs` in the cross-repo E2E job with the org's shared [`capture-docker-logs`](https://github.com/openmrs/openmrs-contrib-gha-workflows/blob/main/.github/actions/capture-docker-logs/action.yml) action, added in [openmrs-contrib-gha-workflows#60](https://github.com/openmrs/openmrs-contrib-gha-workflows/pull/60). It does the same thing: it writes each container's logs to `logs/<container name>.log` for the upload step that follows.

`jwalton/gh-docker-logs` declares the Node 20 runtime, which GitHub [removed from hosted runners](https://github.blog/changelog/2025-09-19-deprecation-of-node-20-on-github-actions-runners/) on September 23. Runners now force it onto Node 24 and log a deprecation warning on each cross-repo E2E job. It hasn't had a release since v2.2.2 in January 2024, so there's no Node 24 version to upgrade to.

If capturing one container's logs fails, the shared action logs a warning and moves on to the next container instead of failing.

## Summary
Logout now clears the shared SWR cache that O3 apps read. Before, it called SWR's global `mutate`, which targets SWR's default cache, so it cleared nothing apps use. Logout goes to the login page without a reload, so the next user in the same tab saw the previous user's cached data before it revalidated.

`RedirectLogout` now passes `cache` and `mutate` from `useSWRConfig()` to `performLogout`, which clears each cached key by name. We need to clear by name because `mutate(() => true)` skips `useSWRInfinite` and `useSWRSubscription` keys, so infinite lists (like the service queues waiting list) would still leak.

## Screenshots

## Related Issue

## Other
To reproduce on `main`:

1. Log in and open the service queues page so the SWR cache fills up.
2. Log out.
3. Inspect the shared SWR cache from the console (for example, find the `SWRConfig` provider's `cache` through React DevTools). Every entry still holds the previous user's data.
4. Log in as another user and open the same page. The previous user's data renders until the refetch comes back. Throttling the network in DevTools makes this easy to see.

With this PR, every entry has `data: undefined` by the time the login page loads, including the `$inf$` keys that `useSWRInfinite` uses.

Since then, `uuid` only resolves by accident. The `openmrs` CLI depends on `webpack-dev-server`, which pulls in `sockjs`, which depends on `uuid@8.3.2`. Module not found: Can't resolve 'uuid' in '.../node_modules/@openmrs/esm-styleguide/dist/workspaces2'

I reproduced that by building the app shell from a copy of a clean `openmrs@next` install with `uuid` only under `sockjs`. Then I installed this branch's styleguide, packed with `yarn pack`, into the same tree. npm put `uuid@11.1.1` where the styleguide can find it, and the build succeeded.

This uses `uuid` 11 rather than the 9 that `esm-offline` declared, because 11 is still supported (npm flags 10 and below as deprecated) and ships its own types.

2. save it as the user's default location preference, and

## Summary

`openmrs develop` can't start on a machine with IPv6 disabled. `isPortAvailable` binds each port on `localhost` and then on `::1`, and treats any error from the `::1` bind as the port being taken. Without IPv6, that bind fails with `EAFNOSUPPORT` for every port, so:

- `openmrs develop --port 8090` exits with "Port 8090 is already in use".
- `openmrs develop` without `--port` checks every port from 8080 to 65535 and then gives up with "Could not find an available port between 8080 and 65535".

I noticed this running the CLI in an IPv4-only container.

This PR only treats the `::1` bind as a conflict when something is actually there. `EAFNOSUPPORT` (IPv6 disabled) and `EADDRNOTAVAIL` (IPv6 enabled but no `::1` on the loopback interface) now fall back to the IPv4 result, which has already passed by that point. Both codes have a unit test, and both tests fail without the fix.

Tested in the same IPv4-only container with the rebuilt CLI:

| | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `openmrs develop --port 8090` | "Port 8090 is already in use" | Starts on 8090 |
| `openmrs develop` | Fails after checking every port | Starts on 8080 |
| `--port` pointing at a port that's actually in use | "already in use" | "already in use" |

body:

- [x] This PR has a title that briefly describes the work done including the ticket number. If there is a ticket, make sure your PR title includes a [conventional commit](https://o3-docs.openmrs.org/en-US/docs/frontend-modules/contributing/#contributing-guidelines) label. - [x] My work includes tests or is validated by existing tests.
- [ ] I have updated the esm-framework and storybook mocks to reflect any API changes. — N/A, no public API change; both changed lines are inside existing global handlers.

## Summary

`window.onerror` and `window.onunhandledrejection` passed their raw `error` / `event.reason` argument straight into `dispatchToastShown` as `description`. When the value was an `Error` object, React could not render it as a child — `ActionableNotification`'s subtitle expects a `ReactNode` — so the toast threw during render and the user saw nothing at all. The failure was silent from the user's perspective, which is the worst case for an error reporter.

Both handlers now go through a small `toToastDescription()` helper, which runs the value through the module's existing `ensureErrorObject()` and returns `.message` only when it is a non-empty string, falling back to the handler's default text otherwise.

`console.error` still receives the raw value, so nothing is lost for debugging.

### Why the message is re-checked rather than just used

The obvious patch is `ensureErrorObject(error).message ?? 'Oops! ...'`, keeping the operator that was already there. That is wrong twice over.

`ensureErrorObject()` returns an `Error` unchanged when it is given one, so whatever that `Error` carries is what reaches the toast:

- `new Error('').message` is `''`. An empty string is not nullish, so `??` lets it through and renders a blank toast — the same "user sees nothing" bug this PR is meant to fix, just quieter. `||` handles that.
- `Error#message` is an ordinary writable property, so it is not guaranteed to be a string at all. An `Error` carrying a truthy non-string message passes straight through `||` as well, and an object is exactly what React cannot render. Thanks to @greptile-apps for catching this one.

`toToastDescription()` therefore checks `typeof message === 'string' && message`, which collapses both cases into one condition. Both shapes have tests against both handlers.

## Screenshots

## Related Issue

https://openmrs.atlassian.net/browse/O3-5981

## Testing

Added 14 cases, covering seven reason shapes against each handler:

| Reason | Resulting toast description |
| --- | --- |
| `new Error('boom')` | `boom` |

## Summary
The app shell's production build minifies CSS with rspack's default Lightning CSS minimizer, which we never give browser targets. On its own defaults Lightning CSS downlevels every logical property in the shell's CSS, and that CSS includes all of Carbon, so each `border-inline-start`, `padding-inline-end` and so on becomes physical properties guarded by `:not(:is(:lang(ae), :lang(ar), ...)))`, repeated for `:-webkit-any` and `:-moz-any`, plus mirrored rules for RTL languages. On `main` that is 6,594 fallback rules, about two thirds of 3 MB of CSS, for browsers that predate our browserslist by years.

The shared rspack and webpack configs for modules already pass `browserslist-config-openmrs` to their CSS minimizers (#1869). The shell config was missed. This adds the same `minimizer` array to the shell's `optimization` block, reusing the `browserTargets` the config already hands to swc. `minimizer` replaces rspack's default pair rather than extending it, so the JS minimizer is listed alongside.

The styleguide stylesheet is marked as already minified. The config compiles it with sass, names it `openmrs.<hash>.css` after a hash of that output, and copies it in as a static file. Minifying it afterwards changed its bytes under a name that no longer matched them, which matters because it's served with a one-year `max-age`; this change alone would have shipped a very different file under the same URL. Sass already emits it compressed, so the copy pattern sets `info.minimized` and the minimizer leaves it alone. That costs about 3 KB gzipped and the filename now matches the bytes it serves.

Built from the same commit before and after:

| | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fallback rules, all shell CSS | 6,594 | 0 |
| All shell CSS, raw | 3.03 MB | 1.11 MB |
| Main stylesheet, gzipped | 163 KB | 104 KB |
| JS output | | byte-identical; only the entry file's hash moves, because it embeds the renamed CSS chunk names |

Logical properties now come through as written, the `:-moz-any` and `:-webkit-any` prefixes are gone, and direction resolves from `dir` the way our `html[dir='rtl']` overrides already assume, instead of from `lang`.

## Screenshots

## Related Issue

## Other
The minimizer honours the targets: the same one-rule build emits fallbacks for `chrome 60`, none for `chrome 120`, output identical to `chrome 120` for `browserslist-config-openmrs`, and fails on an invalid query. Distros pick this up with the next `@openmrs/esm-app-shell` release, since the `openmrs build` command requires the shell's `rspack.config.js`.

Moving the styleguide compilation out of the config factory altogether is left to O3-5966.

## Summary
<!-- Please describe what problems your PR addresses. -->

Another single-spa fix building on the framework timeouts work.

When single-spa bootstraps or unmounts a parcel and the promise rejects due to w/e error, single-spa retains the parcel in its internal registry, including the props. The most expensive part of this is that single-spa can wind up retaining the `domElement` the parcel belongs to, which might actually be large depending on the content of the parcel. We can't clean-up single-spa's internal registry (and there's some value in being able to see broken parcels in its dev tools), but we own the props that we pass to single-spa which single-spa uses to store the `domElement`, so here, if unmounting fails, we release the props, including the `domElement`.

Basically, this reduces the memory pressure from having a bunch of "ghost" single-spa parcels hanging around at the cost of needing to copy the props passed.

This tries to preserve the semantics of rejections still winding up in the global reject handler.

## Summary
<!-- Please describe what problems your PR addresses. -->

In #1856, I added "hard" timeouts of 15s where if a parcel doesn't complete its bootstrap, mount, or unmount call within that time frame, we simply fail it since it would appear to be hung (the boostrap, mount, and unmount calls generally don't load scripts, so the time out here was intended to be a measure of pure JS speed). single-spa provides a mechanism for configuring timeouts like this which #1856 used, with the idea that we could use this to coordinate both single-spa clean-up and the framework's own clean-up. This turned out to be a mistake.

single-spa's "timeouts" actually become `setTimeout()` calls that are not cleared, even when the event they are waiting for has already happened. E.g., the 15s timeout for unmount means that single-spa retains a timeout closure for 15s, even if the unmount operation succeeds faster that that. These timeouts closed over the parcel definitions, including DOM nodes and event listeners, so effectively this change meant that any unmounted extension, modal or workspace was retained in JS memory for 15s, even though the unmount operation itself is normally milliseconds.

By moving the hard timeouts into our framework and reverting to single-spa's defaults, we greatly reduce the window that single-spa will hold the references to its default of 3s. Short of patching single-spa, this seems like the best way we can work around this issue.

NB You'll notice this also uses `setTimeout()`; the difference is that we track this timeout and call `clearTimeout()` if the promise settles.

## Summary
<!-- Please describe what problems your PR addresses. -->

This fixes a major request amplification issue with `useVisit` and `useVisitContextStore`. First, `useVisit` called the `useVisitContextStore` hook twice on every render, first to get some data and then to register a `mutateVisit` callback. Instead, we register a ref as the callback and fill in the refs contents with the actual function, so that `useVisit` only writes to the store once.

More critically, registering the callback required updating the store's state, which triggered re-renders in unrelated components just because we were registering a new `useVisit` hook. Measured with a test, 400 components using `useVisit` would cause 80,600 renders. Likewise, every call to `mutateVisit()`, because it was bound as an action, actually _writes_ to the store, causing re-renders even before invalidating the SWR cache.

Moving the callback tracking out of the store and into a global variable removes both of these re-render amplifications. Re-renders now should only occur when the active visit (or retrospective visit) is updated.

`mutateVisitCallbacks` has been removed from the VisitStoreState; I _think_ it's ok to treat the contents of the store as an internal detail. The implementation surface (including `useVisitContextStore()`) is identical.

## Summary
<!-- Please describe what problems your PR addresses. -->

This is an attempt to reduce much of the churn described here: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/14b92358-1ef6-4152-a4ec-d220bae9e03e.

### PR Overview

This PR overhauls the extension system's internal recomputation model to eliminate O(n²) behavior where any single write (a config change, an extension registering, a slot mounting) triggered a full re-derivation of state for every module, extension, and slot in the app. Derived state is now cached per-entity keyed on its actual inputs, and stores only publish a new value when it actually changed, so consumers no longer re-render on unrelated updates elsewhere in the app. The config system's implementer-tools output is now computed lazily on read instead of eagerly on every write. This is a breaking change to the shape and timing of internal store updates.

Alongside that, the branch clarifies the extension system's data model by splitting what was previously a single "extension" concept into a registration (what a module registers, by name) and a rendering (one live, on-screen copy of a configured instance in a slot — since one instance can render many times, e.g. once per row in a list). Renderings are tracked in their own store, mutated in place for performance rather than copied on every mount/unmount. This also adds support for a per-rendering displayConditionExpression, evaluated against that specific rendering's local state rather than globally. Supporting hooks (useAssignedExtensions, useExtensionSlot, useStore, and a new useShallowStableValue) and Extension.tsx were updated to work with this model, along with substantial new test coverage validating the recomputation and config-propagation behavior.

### Relation to performance

The extension system recomputation this ameliorates is a cause of many of the performance issues we're aiming to fix, but not all of them. Specifically, this should mostly reduce re-render churn, reduce the CPU drag from constant re-computation, and save a little bit of memory due to reshaping of the store's internals. It does not, by itself, resolve all the performance short-comings.

### Notable breakages

* Store no longer tracks `assignedExtensions`. Instead, the store tracks `candidateExtensions`, which is the list of extensions assigned to a slot but which have not had their `Display conditions` `expression` property evaluated yet. This is because the evaluation has the ability to read the extension slot state, which can be different per instance of an extension slot. Use `getAssignedExtensions()` or `useAssignedExtensions()` to get the correct list.
* Relatedly `useAssignedExtensionIds()` is now implemented in terms of `useAssignedExtensions()` and has been deprecated as it is no longer a "fast-path" to get extension metadata.
* `useStore()` no longer returns a copy of the store's state, but the state directly. Use with caution.

## Summary

Two lookups in the docs workflows only ever saw the first page of results.

`gh api` returns 30 items per page, so an approval past the first 30 reviews was invisible to the docs-build preflight, which aborted with "No write-access approval present". [#1819](https://github.com/openmrs/openmrs-esm-core/pull/1819) hit this: 65 reviews, with both approvals at positions 64 and 65. No retry path could go green because the approval, push, and on-demand rebuild paths all share that lookup.

The check-run lookup had the same blind spot. #1819's head SHA has exactly 30 check runs, which is exactly the page size, and a recent `main` SHA has 118, so `Docs / Regenerated` can easily fall outside page 1.

Both lookups now paginate. `gh` applies `--jq` per page, and `--slurp` cannot be combined with `--jq`, so the review loop dedupes with `sort -u` instead of jq's `unique`, and the check-run lookups count matches with `wc -l` instead of jq's `length`, which would otherwise emit one count per page. `per_page=100` keeps the review lookup to a single request.

The check-run lookups also pass `check_name`, which filters server-side, so they stay at one request whatever else the SHA has accumulated. `--method GET` is load-bearing there: without it, `-f` makes the request a POST and it 404s.

I verified both shapes against live data. The review lookup finds the approval where the old one returned nothing. The check-run lookup returns 1 on #1823's head, which has a real successful `Docs / Regenerated`, and 0 on #1819's, which has none.

## Summary
<!-- Please describe what problems your PR addresses. -->

This adds a few options to the `build` subcommand of the `openmrs` CLI to automatically generate pre-compressed versions of all `.js`, `.mjs`, `.cjs`, `.css`, `.json`, `.svg`, `.html`, and `.map` files if compressing the file will save disk space.

Currently, in the RefApp and module-spa, we serve most files using real-time gzip compression, meaning the server applies gzip compression for each request. This wastes CPU cycles since the files served themselves are static. Additionally, because this is done on-the-fly, the level of compression applied is minimal (equivalent to `gzip -1`). Additionally, we miss out on [Brotli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brotli) compression, which is supported by all major browsers and generally provides better compression ratios than gzip for web assets. 

Compressed artifacts are on by default with the `build` command but can be turned _off_ by passing `--no-compress`. Similarly, specific versions can be turned off by `--no-compress-brotli` or `--no-compress-gzip`. This applies the maximum level of both gzip and brotli compression.

This PR is designed to output files in a format that can be consumed, without modification, by nginx's `gzip_static` directive and a future PR will add a similar implementation to module-spa, allowing us to serve frontend assets in smaller bundles.

For the Reference Application, there are 12.7 MB of assets on disk and compressed these become 2.4 MB (gzip) or 1.9 MB (brotli). Note, though that with both nginx and module-spa, we do gzip compress by default, but these numbers still compare favorably to the current size of 2.9 MB for all assets using the lowest level of gzip compression.

One thing I could use a second opinion on: the code will in some cases automatically "clean-up" after itself, e.g., if `file1.js` in one version compresses well, so that `file1.js.gz` and `file1.js.br` are generated, but then `file1.js` is changed so that it doesn't compress well (or is under the 1 kB minimum for compression to be applied), the `file1.js.gz` and `file1.js.br` files will be automatically removed on the next build. The user menu's language item crashes too, as soon as the menu opens. ## Description The session endpoint reports `locale` and `allowedLocales` in Java's `Locale#toString()` form (`en_US`, `sw_KE`). Those aren't valid BCP 47 tags, and `Intl.DisplayNames` throws instead of degrading when handed one. Both the modal and the user menu language item pass the session values to `Intl.DisplayNames` raw. The framework normalizes underscores when it sets `document.lang`, but it never writes that back to the session store and never touches `allowedLocales`, so these components see the raw form. We ship regional translation bundles (`en_US`, `sw_KE`, `pt_BR`, `zh_CN`), so this hits supported configurations. In this PR I have: - Added `toLanguageTag` and `getLocaleDisplayName` helpers that normalize before calling `Intl`, and fall back to the raw identifier for anything `Intl` still rejects - Used them in both components. The outbound value is unchanged, the backend still gets the underscore form it expects, and a test covers the round trip by selecting `sw_KE` and asserting the POSTed value - Fixed the modal swallowing failed updates. `handleSubmit` never awaited the request, so a rejection left the spinner running forever with nothing shown. It now awaits and shows the backend's message, the same way the change password modal does - Made the last locale in a long list visible. The list had a max-height with no overflow, so past roughly nine locales it overflowed into the ModalBody, and Carbon's scroll fade mask kept the last entry invisible even at full scroll (still clickable, though). The list now scrolls itself, with an end margin so the fade lands on empty space on short viewports. There's no unit test for this one since it's CSS layout; the screenshots below are the evidence One thing this doesn't fix: selecting `uz@Latn` still fails, because the session POST parses the submitted value with `LocaleUtils.toLocale`, which rejects both `uz@Latn` and `uz-Latn`. Supporting it needs a backend change in webservices.rest. The modal now at least shows that error instead of hanging. ## Screenshots Captured against a local dev server with the session's `allowedLocales` stubbed to include regional locales; the backend was not modified. ### Before #### On main with an `en_US` session: RangeError from ChangeLanguageLink as soon as the app loads #### "Italiano" obscured from view at the end of the locales list ### After #### User menu rendering the current languag

- Removed 20 stale `eslint-disable` directives across 15 files. ESLint 9 reports unused directives by default, where v8 silently ignored them. Most were artifacts of the typescript-eslint v8 rule renames that the legacy config never accounted for. These are comment and whitespace-only changes.

The styleguide's global `.cds--btn--primary` override loads after Carbon's `.cds--copy-btn` rule and ties it on specificity, so it wins on source order. As a result, every Carbon CodeSnippet copy button in O3 renders as a solid brand-teal primary button instead of Carbon's subtle layer-background icon button. This first surfaced in the TOTP enrollment modal in #1819. This PR excludes the copy button from the override using `:not(:where(.cds--copy-btn))`. The zero-specificity `:where()` keeps the override selectors at (0,1,0) specificity. A plain `:not(.cds--copy-btn)` would raise them to (0,2,0), which would beat Carbon's `.cds--btn:disabled` rule at (0,1,1) and repaint disabled primary buttons teal. Verified against the compiled styleguide CSS and the built app shell bundle: the copy button now gets Carbon's layer background at rest, layer-hover on hover, layer-active on active, and Carbon's own focus outline, in both light and dark (g100) themes. ## Summary

`ActiveWorkspaceWindow` loads workspace lifecycles asynchronously and stored them in an array that the render reads by stack index. When the stack changes shape in quick succession, for example a child workspace closes and a different one opens at the same position, the newly opened workspace can be handed the previous workspace's lifecycle from the stale array. Since the parcel mounts whatever config it first receives and ignores later config changes, the wrong component then renders permanently, with the new workspace's definition props. Every workspaceProp the component destructures is undefined at that point.

We hit this in the ward app's "Add patient to ward" flow: the start visit form closes on save and immediately launches the admission workspace, which then rendered a blank visit form (the closed workspace's component) instead of the admission UI, firing requests like `GET /ws/rest/v1/patient/undefined` from hooks that received undefined props. Whether it reproduced depended on whether the close and the launch landed in the same React commit.

This change keys the loaded lifecycles by the opened workspace's uuid, so a stale entry is unreachable by construction: a newly opened workspace has a fresh uuid and shows the loading placeholder until its own lifecycle resolves. The load effect also ignores resolutions from superseded runs so an out of order resolution cannot clobber the current map.

The included test replaces the workspace at a stack position while the replacement's lifecycle is still loading and asserts the stale component is not mounted. It fails against the previous index-based lookup and passes with this change.

## Summary

`openmrsComponentDecorator` wraps every decorated component in its own `<SWRConfig>` that points at a single module-level cache (`swrCache`, added in #1397 to give one global SWR cache regardless of module-federation load order).

SWR ties a provider cache's global state to the lifecycle of the **first** `<SWRConfig>` boundary that initializes it: that boundary's unmount runs `SWRGlobalState.delete(cache)`. Because every decorated component, extension, and workspace mounts its own `<SWRConfig>` over the one shared cache, whichever mounts first owns that deleter. When it unmounts while others are still mounted (routine on a busy page, e.g. navigating the patient chart or closing a workspace), the shared state is removed — the survivors' next render calls `SWRGlobalState.get(cache)`, which now returns `undefined`, and destructuring that throws `TypeError: undefined is not iterable`. The single-spa error boundary then replaces the page with "An error has occurred".

This is a **single-instance lifecycle bug**: it reproduces with one `swr/_internal` instance and no module federation (see the regression test). It is distinct from the separate multi-instance case — a cache registered in one `swr/_internal` instance being read from another — which `singleton: true` is there to prevent.

This is the cause of the intermittent patient-chart e2e failures (a different chart spec fails each run, e.g. `visit-context-navigation`, `drug-orders`, `attachments`, always a chart page timing out because it was replaced by the error boundary).

### Fix

Keep #1397's single shared cache, but **pre-initialize it once at module load** (`initCache(swrCache)`). That transfers ownership of the cache's `SWRGlobalState` from the first `<SWRConfig>` boundary to this (singleton) framework module: every `<SWRConfig>` then takes SWR's "already initialized" path and none of them registers the deleting cleanup, so the shared state is never torn down. This preserves #1397's guarantee of one global cache regardless of load order (and leaves the global `mutate()` behavior unchanged); it does **not** revert to SWR's default cache.

`ComponentDecoratorOptions['swrConfig']` is also tightened to omit `provider` (alongside the already-omitted `fetcher`), so a caller can't accidentally swap in a different cache provider per component. No current caller passes one.

### Tests

Adds `openmrsComponentDecorator.swr-cache.test.tsx`:
- a regression test that mounts two decorated components over the shared cache, unmounts the first (the owner), re-renders the survivor, and asserts it keeps working (fails without the fix, passes with it);
- a test confirming cached data is still shared across separately decorated components.

## Other

This deliberately keeps the single-global-cache design from #1397 (which was introduced to fix data-consistency problems with SWR's default cache under module federation, see #1395 / #774). The only change is to stop binding that cache's life

[The `bundle-size.yml` workflow was failing with](https://github.com/openmrs/openmrs-esm-core/actions/runs/27000979662/job/79681621929):

```
Unable to locate executable file: turbo. Please verify either the file path exists or the file can be found within a directory specified by the PATH environment variable.
```

**Root cause:** `preactjs/compressed-size-action@v3` is a floating tag. On 2026-06-05, the `v3` tag was advanced to a new build that contained a breaking change originally merged in December 2025 ([`feat!: allow to run any script for clean/install/build`](https://github.com/preactjs/compressed-size-action/pull/126)).

This change had two effects:

1. **Auto-install removed:** The action previously auto-detected the package manager from the lockfile and ran `yarn --frozen-lockfile` when a `yarn.lock` was present. The new version removed `getPackageManagerAndInstallScript()` entirely — `install-script` is now fully opt-in and nothing installs if it isn't provided.

2. **Build script execution changed:** The action previously ran the build as `yarn run <build-script>`, which adds `node_modules/.bin` to PATH automatically. The new version executes `build-script` directly via `exec()` with no PATH augmentation, so binaries in `node_modules/.bin` (including `turbo`) are not found even after installing dependencies.

**Fix:** Add `install-script: "yarn install --immutable"` so dependencies are installed, and prefix the build script with `yarn` (`yarn turbo run build --color`) so that `turbo` is resolved through `node_modules/.bin`.

## Summary

The Implementer Tools UI Editor rendered slot overlays but no **extension** overlays, even on pages with many extensions (for example the patient chart, which has dozens of `[data-extension-id]` nodes).

The overlay targets were computed by treating `extensions[name].instances` as a nested object. In the framework extension store that field is `Array<ExtensionInstance>`, so iterating it with `Object.entries` produced array indices (`"0"`) as module names and instance property names (`"id"`, `"slotName"`) as slot names, with an `undefined` instance id. The resulting `data-extension-*` selectors never matched a real DOM node, so no extension overlay rendered even when extensions were present. This PR iterates the instances array directly through a small `getExtensionOverlayTargets` helper that reads `slotName`, `slotModuleName`, and `id` from each instance. (The slot-overlay path was already correct, since `slots` genuinely is a `Record`.)

Fixing that surfaced a latent leak that had been masked while no overlays mounted: `ExtensionOverlay` appends a portal container to the host element's parent on mount but never removed it. With overlays now mounting, exiting the UI Editor or changing the host element orphaned empty sibling divs in the host application's DOM. This adds an effect cleanup that removes the container on unmount and when the host element changes.

Includes regression tests for the traversal helper (`getExtensionOverlayTargets`) and the overlay container lifecycle (no leak on unmount or host change).

This patch adds the missing bridge in the styleguide's overrides so the existing clamp resolves to lg (48px). Design reference: [Carbon Search — Style](https://www.carbondesignsystem.com/components/search/style/) (lg = 48px, matching the lg Button it's paired with).
DevTools evidence (before fix) The `` wrapper carries `cds--search--lg` but the bundled Carbon styles only use that class to position the magnifier icon. No rule sets `--cds-layout-size-height` for the search subtree, so the `clamp()` on `.cds--search-input` resolves to its `md` fallback (40px). ## Summary
<!-- Please describe what problems your PR addresses. -->

Currently, we use a Husky hook to run documentation generation. This process is somewhat slow which leads to many contributors skipping it, resulting both in the docs getting out of date and weird documentation changes ending up in unrelated PRs. Instead of pushing this on the local dev, the goal here is to add docs to PRs as part of a semi-automated workflow.

The way this intended to work:

1. Contributor submits PR
2. If changes are made to files that may affect docs, a check is failed.
3. Reviewers review as normal.
4. Once PR is approved by a user with write access to the repo, a job will spin-up which will generate the updated docs and add them to the PR.
5. At this point the failing check will be moved to success
6. Future commits to the PR (that do not mess with any of the docs workflows) from this point on will automatically trigger rebuilding the docs

There are some additional controls in place around PRs that touch the workflow files requiring approval from a /dev/5 because, of necessity, many of these jobs run in the scope of the PR and malicious changes to these files could result in secrets leaking.

I've done my best to try and ensure that secrets are never visible in a context where user-supplied code is run, which is why many workflows have a large number of tasks or pass things through artifacts.

There's also a fallback to manually trigger the docs and a /dev/5 can label any PR with `skip-docs` to opt-out of every stage of this process.

title: (fix) O3-4020: Return current app context value synchronously on first render
body:
## Requirements

- [x] This PR has a title that briefly describes the work done, including the ticket number if there is a ticket.
- [x] My work conforms to the [OpenMRS 3.0 Styleguide](https://om.rs/styleguide) and [Contributing Guidelines](https://o3-docs.openmrs.org/docs/frontend-modules/contributing.en-US#contributing-guidelines).
- [x] My work includes tests or is validated by existing tests.

## Summary

Addresses [O3-4020](https://openmrs.atlassian.net/browse/O3-4020): `useAppContext` returned `null`/falsy-empty values in `AdmissionRequestsWorkspace` (and, more generally, in any consumer that mounted before the subscription effect fired or after the owner unmounted).

`useAppContext` had two related issues:

1. **First-render race.** `useState<Readonly<U>>()` initialized the local value as `undefined` and was only populated once the `useEffect` subscription fired. On the very first render, consumers received `undefined` even when the namespace was already registered. This is the timing race that produced the symptom reported by @chibongho (cc @ibacher) — the Ward App's `AdmissionRequestsWorkspace` destructured the context before it had arrived.
2. **Owner-unmount shadowing.** `subscribeToContext` substitutes `Object.freeze({})` when a namespace is unregistered (via `Object.assign({}, null)`). The previous implementation forwarded that `{}` straight to `setValue`, so after the namespace owner (e.g. `DefaultWardView` / `MaternalWardView`) unmounted, every consumer held a truthy empty object instead of `undefined`. Destructuring that object yielded `undefined` properties and required defensive `?? {}` guards — exactly the workaround present in `admission-requests.workspace.tsx`.

### Fix

- Seed the `useState` initializer by calling `getContext(namespace)` synchronously, so the first render already has the current value (or `undefined` when the namespace is absent).
- Inside the subscription callback, prefer the `state` argument forwarded by `subscribeToContext` to avoid re-reading/cloning the context on every update. Fall back to `getContext` only for the ambiguous empty-object case, and set the local value to `undefined` when the namespace is no longer registered.
- Share a small `isBlankNamespace` helper between the state initializer and the validation effect so whitespace-only namespaces are handled uniformly (`namespace.trim().length === 0` rather than `replace(' ', '')`, which only trimmed a single space).

### Tests (new file `useAppContext.test.tsx`)

- Returns `undefined` when the namespace is not registered.
- Returns the currently-registered value on the very first render.
- Applies the selector on the first render.
- Exposes a sibling `useDefineAppContext` value to the consumer after effects flush.
- Returns `undefined` (not `{}`) after the namespace owner unmounts (the O3-4020 scenario).

All 5 new tests pass; full `@openmrs/esm-react-utils` suite remains green (125 passed, 9 skipped).

### Behavior changes

| Scenario | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First render, namespace already registered | `undefined` | registered value |
| First render, namespace not registered | `{}` eventually | `undefined` |
| Owner unmounts while consumer mounted | `{}` (frozen) | `undefined` |
| Steady state (owner mounted, value updates) | updated value | updated value |

The default selector `(state) => (state ?? {}) as Readonly<U>` is preserved; it is now only invoked when the state is a real, registered value.

## Screenshots

N/A — this is a behavioral fix in a framework hook; no visible UI changes. Verified via unit tests covering the first-render, selector, sibling-producer, and owner-unmount scenarios.

## Related Issue

https://openmrs.atlassian.net/browse/O3-4020

## Other

The Ward App's `?? {}` defensive workaround in `admission-requests.workspace.tsx` continues to function and remains in place — it is now correctly redundant for the registered case and correctly guards against a genuinely absent owner.

This needs a lot of explanations. We use a series of early-days hacks to support [import maps](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Elements/script/type/importmap) in O3. We use these import maps primarily to find the scripts that implement the different microfrontend containers ("apps"). One of these hacks is a library called `import-map-overrides`, which is _primarily_ intended as a developer tool, but which also included some nice functionality not available in default browser implementations of import maps include:

* Support for multiple import maps on a single page
* Support for loading import maps via `<script>` tags with a `src` attribute (which is how we currently do things)

It also provides tooling that is useful solely in dev-mode, like providing import map entries via `localStorage` and leveraging those to override dependencies defined in the "static" import map included in the page. Unfortunately, supporting the things we want enabled at runtime even in production also meant supporting the things we didn't want running in production at runtime. Additionally, our `routes.registry.json` handling (the main file that describes all of the entry points that a microfrontend provides to the framework) is built on the model of `import-map-overrides` as so has the exact same issues.

Essentially, because of the way things were working, and import map overrides or route overrides that are stored in `localStorage` would be incorporated into the effective import map or effective route registry, even in production mode, which means that these could be used by someone to unexpectedly load a remote definition of a microfrontend (preventing this is one of the reasons that the RefApp runs with a reasonably strict Content Security Policy). This type of tooling is great in dev mode when we actually do want to load scripts from remote locations (locally running microfrontends).

In order to keep the functions that we want in production mode while only allowing the `localStorage` overrides in development mode, it was necessary to remove the `import-map-overrides` and replace it with our own shim that maintains the same API but where we can selectively disable parts of it.

We further have a feature, `spaEnv`, which has been part of the framework for a while without actively being used for anything which allows implementations to declare whether an instance is intended for "development", "test", or "production". In "production" mode (the default), the framework will not load any import map overrides or routes overrides. This also means that this PR deprecates the ability to access the import map overrides via `localStorage`.

## Summary

`useLocationCount` in `location-picker.resource.ts` used `String.prototype.concat()` to append the `_tag=Login Location` FHIR filter when `useLoginLocationTag` was enabled.  However, `concat()` returns a new string without mutating the original, so the tag  filter was silently never applied regardless of the config value.

This meant any deployment using login-location tagging was unknowingly counting all locations instead of only tagged ones. Because `chooseLocation.useLoginLocationTag` defaults to `true`, this affected the default configuration, not only sites that explicitly opted in. As a result, `locationCount` returned the total location count rather than the tagged count, which broke the auto-redirect logic that skips the location picker when only one valid login location exists.

**Changes made:**
- Replaced `url.concat()` with `URLSearchParams` which correctly builds and encodes 
  the query string, consistent with `useLoginLocations()` in `login.resource.ts`
- Corrected FHIR parameter name from `tag=` to `_tag=` which is the correct FHIR R4 
  parameter name
- Added unit tests for `useLocationCount` covering URL construction for both flag 
  values, response shape, and the null `firstLocation` edge case

## Screenshots

No UI changes. The fix corrects a silent data-fetching bug. The location picker screen behaviour changes only for sites using login-location tagging (the default),  where the correct tagged location count is now returned from the server.
